title: Context of the Research
text:
The Digital Health Paradox
Digital health technologies — health apps, wearable trackers, and online health services — have become a routine part of life for millions of people in the UK. Policymakers have positioned them as cost-effective tools for improving population health at scale (Rich, 2019; Mariano, 2020; Steinhubl, 2013), and the NHS Ten Year Plan has made the shift to digital healthcare a core strategic priority (Department of Health and Social Care, 2025).
Yet the benefits of digital health are not equally shared. People from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, older adults, and other disadvantaged groups are consistently less likely to benefit from digital health interventions — even when access to technology is not the issue (Western, 2021; Zhang, 2023; Birch, 2022; Badr, 2024). This is sometimes called the digital health paradox: technologies designed to improve health for everyone may, in practice, widen existing health inequalities.

title: Context of the Research
text:
Why Do Inequalities Persist?
Researchers have identified three levels at which digital divides operate (van Dijk, 2020):

Level 1 — Material access: who has devices and internet connectivity
Level 2 — Skills and usage: who can use technology effectively
Level 3 — Outcomes: who actually benefits, even after access and skills barriers are overcome

Most existing research and policy has focused on Levels 1 and 2. But outcome inequalities remain even when people have both access and basic skills. One systematic review and meta-analysis found that individuals in the lowest socioeconomic group derived no measurable benefit from digital health interventions for physical activity (Western, 2021). Understanding why requires looking beyond infrastructure and towards the psychological, social, and motivational factors that shape whether someone can truly benefit from digital health.

title: Context of the Research
text:
Existing Frameworks and Their Limits
Several theoretical traditions have contributed to our understanding of digital health engagement. Cognitive and motivational theories — including Social Cognitive Theory (Bandura, 1991) and Self-Determination Theory (Ryan, 1997) — offer accounts of how self-efficacy, motivation, and behavioural regulation shape health behaviour. Technology adoption models such as the Technology Acceptance Model (Davis, 1989) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (Venkatesh, 2003) explain initial adoption decisions based on perceived usefulness and ease of use. Digital health literacy frameworks such as eHEALS (Norman, 2006) capture individuals’ ability to find, evaluate, and apply digital health information. Structural and sociocultural frameworks — including Diffusion of Innovation Theory (Rogers, 2014), Domestication Theory (Silverstone, 1993), and ecological models such as the Digital Health Rainbow (Jahnel, 2022) — situate digital health use within broader social and material contexts.
No single framework, however, integrates these domains into a coherent, measurable account of why some people benefit from digital health and others do not.

title: Context of the Research
text:
Introducing Digital Health Enablement
Digital Health Enablement (DHE) is a new psychological construct developed to address this gap, defined as:

An individual’s readiness and capability to use, engage with, and benefit from digital technologies for the purpose of maintaining health, preventing ill health, or in the management of health conditions.

We use the term enablement deliberately — to signal that variation in who benefits from digital health reflects not individual deficit, but differential access to the conditions that make capability real (Zheng, 2008). DHE is conceived as dimensional (not an all-or-nothing state), dynamic (varying with time, context, and circumstance), and relational (someone may be well-enabled to use a laptop but not a smartwatch).
DHE is structured around a progression through three levels: use, engagement, and benefit. Seven psychosocial sub-constructs shape an individual’s capacity to progress through this pathway, each modifiable through targeted support or intervention design. These proximal factors are shaped in turn by more distal influences — economic circumstances, cultural environment, and personal characteristics such as values, personality, and physical health. By assessing DHE, it becomes possible to identify where support is needed and to tailor digital health interventions accordingly.

title: The Theory of DHE
text:
The Digital Health Enablement (DHE) model proposes that an individual’s capacity to benefit from digital health interventions is shaped by seven inter-related domains. These domains capture the cognitive, social, and behavioural factors that determine whether a person can meaningfully engage with digital health tools.
The model situates these domains within a broader context of structural drivers — economic, social, cultural, and personal factors — that shape enablement upstream. Together, greater enablement across these domains is theorised to predict improved uptake, engagement, and effectiveness of digital health interventions.



Figure 1 The Digital Health Enablement model (Mercer, et al., 2026)



Table 1 DHE Sub-Constructs Definitions






Sub-Construct
Definition




Digital Skills
Perception of one’s abilities to effectively engage and use digital technologies safely in areas including health information gathering, communication, content creation, and problem solving


Digital Health Literacy
The extent to which one understands digital technologies and approaches digital health resources critically, including in the selection, evaluation, and application of digital technologies


Digital Self-Efficacy
The extent to which individuals are confident in their ability to use digital technologies effectively


Sociodigital Norms
The behaviours around digital technologies that are either typical or seen as proper in each context


Digital Outcome Expectancy
An individual’s beliefs about the likely physical, social, or self-evaluative outcomes of engaging with digital health technologies


Digital Trust
The confidence that users have in the integrity, security, and privacy of digital technologies


Digital Behavioural Regulation
The extent to which individual behaviours around digital health technologies are regulated by internal or external factors

title: Measuring DHE
text:
The Digital Health Enablement Scale (DHES) is a self-report psychometric instrument designed to measure an individual’s capacity to engage with and benefit from digital health interventions. It operationalises the seven domains of the DHE model, capturing the cognitive, motivational, social, and behavioural factors that underpin meaningful digital health engagement.



Figure 2 Stages of DHES development (adapted from Boateng et al., 2018).


The scale is designed for use with adult populations in research and clinical contexts, with particular relevance to settings where digital health inequalities are a concern — including primary care, public health, and weight-related behaviour change programmes.

title: Measuring DHE
text:
Current Status
The DHES is currently undergoing peer review. A full validation study examining the scale’s structural validity, reliability, and convergent validity in a UK adult sample is ongoing.
The scale is not yet publicly available. Researchers interested in the DHES — including those wishing to collaborate or discuss potential applications — are warmly encouraged to get in touch.

title: Digital Health Enablement
text:
The Digital Health Divide
Digital health technologies such as health apps and wearables offer enormous potential to improve health and extend the reach of healthcare. Yet their benefits are unequally distributed.
Factors including digital skills, health literacy, self-efficacy, socio-digital norms and trust shape whether individuals can meaningfully engage with, and benefit from, digital health — and these factors cluster in ways that deepen existing health inequalities.
Find out more about digital health inequality here.


The DHE Project






What is Digital Health Enablement (DHE)?



DHE is the constellation of individual-level factors that determine whether a person is positioned to meaningfully engage with and benefit from digital health interventions. It encompasses the skills, knowledge, motivation, and social context that shape an individual’s capacity to use digital health tools effectively.


The Digital Health Enablement (DHE) project is a programme of doctoral research based at the University of Bath, developing and validating a new psychometric instrument — the Digital Health Enablement Scale (DHES) — designed to measure individual-level enablement for digital health engagement.
The DHE project is based in the Centre for Motivation and Health Behaviour Change within the Department of Health at the University of Bath. The research is supervised by Dr Max Western, Dr Roberta Bernardi (University of Bristol), and Professor Martyn Standage.
